title: Look closer
hookLine: you'd travel to Olympia to see Phidias' statue, so why not look at the world's order? (Discourses 1.6)

lines: ACROSS THE WORLD FOR A PAINTING.
A FEW MOMENTS IN A CROWD.
cards: People fly across the world to stand in a crowd in front of a well-known painting for a few moments. They wait in line, they get jostled, they hold their phones over strangers' heads.

Then they go home and walk past the sky every evening without looking up. Nobody plans a trip to see their own street at dusk. Epictetus saw the same thing in his own century, with a statue instead of a painting.

teach.b: The statue was Phidias' Zeus at Olympia. People travel to Olympia to see Phidias' work, Epictetus says, still in Discourses book one, chapter six, and think it a misfortune to die without having seen it.
Then comes the turn. You don't have to travel at all to see the works he finds more marvelous: the world itself, and its order. It's here already.
And you'd rather not look? But life is hard, someone says. And Olympia isn't? he answers.
The heat. The crowds pressing in. Nowhere decent to wash.
Getting soaked when it rains. The noise and the shouting. People put up with all of it, because the sight is worth it.
Earlier in the same chapter he says why humans are here at all. Animals simply live.
But a human was brought into the world to be a spectator of it, and more than a spectator, an interpreter: someone who looks and understands and says what they see.
To finish your life without ever really looking, he says, is to miss the reason you came. That's the Stoic view, built on their belief in a reasoning God. The practice in it needs no belief at all.
The marvel you'd cross an ocean for may be on your windowsill.

how: Some readers of Epictetus turn this chapter into a habit of deliberate looking: a minute each day spent with one ordinary thing as if it were a well-known work of art.

o: giving the everyday world the look you'd give a wonder
studying a well-known artwork until you know every detail
peering at the small print before you sign

s: Epictetus says the trip to Olympia was comfortable
he lists the heat, the crowds, the bad washing and the rain.
he says humans came into the world to be spectators and interpreters of it
not just to live, but to look and to understand.
Epictetus says people think it a misfortune to die without seeing Phidias' work
they cross the heat and crowds to see one statue; the world's order is already here.

games.q: you've survived the heat and the crowds at Olympia and seen the great statue. what does Epictetus ask you next?
o: why won't you look at the world's order, which is already here?
did it live up to the hype?
games.why: he turns from the statue to the world itself: you'd travel for one, and you won't look at the other.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing within reach, a leaf, your own palm, the grain of a table, the light on a wall, and look at it as if you'd traveled a long way and waited in a crowd to see it: its color, its edges, how the light sits on it.
When your mind wanders, bring it back the way a tourist would, because you came all this way.

wordCard.voice: Look closer. Epictetus' challenge: we'd suffer crowds and heat to see one statue, while the order of the world sits in front of us every day.

orig.note: Greek theatēs: spectator, one who watches (our word theater shares the root); Epictetus says humans came into the world to be spectators and interpreters.

carryVoice: Your line: looks and understands. A spectator, and more than that, an interpreter. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.6 (of providence: Olympia; spectator and interpreter)
